phases: Pluecker homogeneous line coordinates and duality

milestones.label: Moebius introduces barycentric (homogeneous) coordinates
milestones.work: A. F. Moebius, Der barycentrische Calcul, Leipzig, 1827
milestones.description: Moebius describes each point of the plane by weights placed at the vertices of a triangle, giving homogeneous coordinates that also cover points at infinity.

evidence.claim: Digitised copy of the 1827 Leipzig edition of the book exists in the archive catalogue.
Article attributes the introduction of homogeneous coordinates to Moebius in his 1827 work.
Biography says the 1827 book introduced homogeneous coordinates and projective transformations.
Topic page shows every plane point fixed by weights [a,b,c] at triangle vertices.

milestones.label: Mobius titles his book with the barycentric-calculus name
milestones.work: Mobius, A. F., Der barycentrische Calcul, 1827
milestones.description: The first title found using "barycentric calculus", an alias for the event.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the title with first publication year 1827

milestones.note: Name is the event alias, not the modern "homogeneous coordinates" label. The zbMATH entry is searched by title, its id was not kept.

milestones.phase: Pluecker homogeneous line coordinates and duality
milestones.label: Pluecker uses homogeneous line coordinates for conics
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, Analytisch-geometrische Entwickelungen, vol. 2, Essen, 1831
milestones.description: In the second volume Pluecker treats conics as envelopes of lines using homogeneous line coordinates, making duality a matter of symbolic calculation.

evidence.claim: Biography summarises vol. 1 (1828) with affine point coordinates and vol. 2 (three years later) with homogeneous line coordinates.

milestones.note: No bibliographic record for the 1831 volume was found in Crossref or the archive.org catalogue searched, so evidence stays at history_page level.

milestones.phase: Pluecker homogeneous line coordinates and duality
milestones.label: Pluecker's system of analytic geometry with point and line coordinates
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, System der analytischen Geometrie, Berlin, 1835
milestones.description: Pluecker uses both point and line coordinates for a detailed theory of plane cubic curves.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1835 System der analytischen Geometrie.
Biography says the book treats point and line coordinates and mainly plane cubics.

milestones.label: Plucker publishes an analytic geometry system with new coordinate methods
milestones.work: Plucker, J., System der analytischen Geometrie, auf neue Betrachtungsweisen gegrundet, 1835
milestones.description: Book-length treatment that introduces new analytic coordinate methods, the basis for later line coordinates.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the book with first publication year 1835

milestones.note: Catalogue year; content on homogeneous and line coordinates not checked page by page.

milestones.phase: Pluecker homogeneous line coordinates and duality
milestones.label: Pluecker's theory of algebraic curves (Pluecker equations)
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, Theorie der algebraischen Curven, Bonn, 1839
milestones.description: The book studies singular points and points at infinity and states the relations between the order and class of a curve, a result of the dual coordinate viewpoint.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1839 Theorie der algebraischen Curven.
Biography says this work contains the equations relating order and class.

people.name: Julius Pluecker
people.roleNote: Line coordinates, duality and curve theory

notes: Sources read: Wikipedia 'Homogeneous coordinates' (raw wikitext), MacTutor biographies of Moebius and Pluecker and the topic page Abstract linear spaces. Wikipedia's Julius Pluecker article could not be retrieved (server error). The first use of the phrase 'homogeneous coordinates' was not found and is left open. The term 'Pluecker coordinates' for line coordinates is later; no dated coinage found. Priority between Moebius (1827) and Pluecker (1828-31) is not argued in the pages read; the 1831 volume year rests on MacTutor only. The saved leads file has no candidates for this event.

canonicalName: Axioms for linear (vector) spaces: Moebius, Grassmann, Peano

milestones.label: Moebius' barycentric calculus with directed quantities
milestones.work: A. F. Moebius, Der barycentrische Calcul, Leipzig, 1827
milestones.description: Moebius places weights at points and works with directed quantities, the idea Grassmann names as his main motivation.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1827 Leipzig book.
Topic page says barycentric weights were an early appearance of vectors and Grassmann's main motivation.

milestones.label: Grassmann's Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre
milestones.work: H. Grassmann, Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre, ein neuer Zweig der Mathematik, Leipzig, 1844
milestones.description: Grassmann builds an abstract calculus of undefined quantities with addition, scalar multiplication and a product, containing independence, dimension and the scalar product.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists an 1844 edition of the book.
Topic page lists linear independence, dimension and the scalar product as present in the 1844 work.
Biography says the manuscript was finished in autumn 1843 and published the next year.

milestones.label: Second, rigorous Ausdehnungslehre
milestones.work: H. Grassmann, Die Ausdehnungslehre: vollstaendig und in strenger Form bearbeitet, 1862
milestones.description: Grassmann rewrites the theory in a more readable and formal version with a long programmatic introduction.

evidence.claim: Topic page dates the more readable second version to 1862 and says the introduction defends its formal method.

milestones.note: Only a history page was used; no 1862 record was found in the archive.org catalogue search.

milestones.label: Hankel recognises Grassmann's work
milestones.work: H. Hankel, Theorie der complexen Zahlensysteme, 1867
milestones.description: Hankel is the first to see the importance of Grassmann's ideas, building abstractly defined number systems on them.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Hankel was first to see the importance of Grassmann's work and cites his 1867 paper.

milestones.label: Peano's axioms for a real linear space
milestones.work: G. Peano, Calcolo geometrico secondo l'Ausdehnungslehre di H. Grassmann, Turin, 1888
milestones.description: In chapter IX Peano gives axioms for a linear space over the reals, allowing infinite dimension and crediting Leibniz, Moebius, Grassmann and Hamilton.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Peano's 1888 book gives the first axiomatic definition of a real linear space.
Article says Peano gave the modern definition in 1888 under the name linear systems and allowed infinite dimension.
Biography says the 1888 book sets out Grassmann's ideas with great clarity.
zbMATH 20.0689.04: Peano, 'Calcolo geometrico secondo l'Ausdehnungslehre di H. Grassmann', Torino 1888.

milestones.note: Evidence is history pages only: the archive.org search found only the 1891 Gli elementi di calcolo geometrico, and Open Library was unreachable.

milestones.label: Pincherle adopts Peano's axioms for infinite dimensions
milestones.work: S. Pincherle, work of 1897 on infinite-dimensional spaces (exact title not checked)
milestones.description: Pincherle takes up Peano's axioms and makes first inroads into infinite-dimensional vector space theory.

evidence.claim: Article says Pincherle adopted Peano's axioms in 1897 and made initial inroads into infinite-dimensional spaces.

milestones.note: Work title not identified; Crossref query returned nothing matching. Keep as a lead.

works.whyItMatters: Contains the laws of vector spaces and exterior algebra.

people.name: Giuseppe Peano

works.citation: Calcolo geometrico secondo l'Ausdehnungslehre di H. Grassmann

people.roleNote: First axioms for a real linear space

notes: Sources read: MacTutor topic page Abstract linear spaces (saved), MacTutor biographies of Peano and Grassmann, Wikipedia 'Vector space' and 'Hermann Grassmann'. Priority disputes with Cauchy and Saint-Venant over Grassmann's ideas (1845, 1853-54) are recorded on the topic page and not resolved. Bolzano (1804), Bellavitis (1832) and Hamilton (1833, 1843) are mentioned there as related precursors but are not entered as milestones. Open question: whether a vector-space axiomatisation exists before Peano 1888 beyond Grassmann's informal formal system; Peano's record is history-page only. Fix pass 2: zbMATH confirms Peano's 'Calcolo geometrico' (Torino 1888); the priority disputes with Cauchy and Saint-Venant remain unresolved.

canonicalName: Jacobi: four squares via elliptic (theta) functions
aliases: Sum of four squares formula r4(n)
phases: Jacobi's counting formula via theta functions

milestones.label: Lagrange proves every integer is a sum of four squares
milestones.work: J.-L. Lagrange, 1770 (existence proof; title and venue not checked)
milestones.description: Lagrange gave the first proof that every natural number is a sum of four squares, the result Jacobi's formula later refines.

evidence.claim: Article says the theorem was proved by Lagrange in 1770.

milestones.label: Jacobi's note 'on decomposing a number into four squares'
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Note sur la decomposition d'un nombre donne en quatre carres, J. reine angew. Math. 3 (1828) 191
milestones.description: The earliest title found that names the four-squares decomposition theme; it appears in Crelle's Journal a year before the 1829 Fundamenta nova.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record 'Note sur la decomposition d'un nombre donne en quatre carres', Jacobi, J. reine angew. Math. 3 (1828) 191
Crossref/DOI record for the same 1828 article (DOI from the zbMATH links)

milestones.note: Title-level naming of the theme, not a coinage of the modern name 'Jacobi's four-square theorem'. It predates the 1829 first_statement already in the record, so the conceptual derived date would move to 1828 if the content of the note confirms the four-square result. The note itself was not read. A reviewer should decide this. Reclassified from naming to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1829) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.phase: Jacobi's counting formula via theta functions
milestones.label: Jacobi's Fundamenta nova gives the number of representations
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, Koenigsberg, 1829
milestones.description: From his theta-function series Jacobi obtains a formula for the number of ways an odd number is a sum of four squares in terms of the sum of its divisors, and notes that Fermat's four-square theorem follows as a corollary.

evidence.claim: Scanned text of the 1829 book ends its main text with a corollary about Fermat's four-square theorem after a divisor-sum formula for odd p.
Biography dates Fundamenta nova to 1829 and says it rests on four theta functions.

milestones.note: Wikipedia gives 1834 as the date of the theorem; the 1829 book already contains the odd-n case in a corollary, so the 1834 paper is listed separately. Counted under both first_statement and first_application because the one book states the formula and derives it from theta functions.

milestones.label: Theta functions applied to sums of squares
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, 1829
milestones.description: The arithmetic count is derived from series expansions of the new elliptic (theta) functions, the transfer of technique from analysis to number theory.

evidence.claim: Same scan: the divisor-sum expression is derived in the elliptic-function text before the corollary.
MacTutor topic page on elliptic functions and integrals (background; does not mention the four-square result).

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement milestone; the derivation steps were not read line by line.

milestones.label: Jacobi's paper on composition of numbers from four squares
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, De compositione numerorum e quatuor quadratis, J. reine angew. Math. 12 (1834) 167-172
milestones.description: A dedicated short paper on the same four-square count; Wikipedia dates the theorem to this year.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 12 and pages 167-172 confirmed, dated 1834.
Article says the theorem was proved in 1834 by Jacobi.

people.name: Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi

works.whyItMatters: Source of the formula as corollary.

works.citation: De compositione numerorum e quatuor quadratis

people.roleNote: Theta functions and the counting formula

works.citation: J. W. L. Glaisher, On the representation of an uneven number as a sum of four squares and as the sum of a square and two triangular numbers, Phil. Mag. (5) 1 (1876) 44-49
works.whyItMatters: A separate later analysis of four-square representations, for odd numbers, in the line opened by Jacobi's theorem.

works.citation: J. W. L. Glaisher, On the representations of a number as a sum of four squares, and on some allied arithmetical functions, Quart. J. Math. 36 (1904) 305-358
works.whyItMatters: A long systematic study of four-square representation numbers and related functions, following Jacobi's formula.

notes: Sources read: Wikipedia 'Jacobi's four-square theorem' and 'Lagrange's four-square theorem', MacTutor biography of Jacobi (no mention of four squares) and topic page Elliptic functions (saved, covers only the early period). Date conflict: Wikipedia 1834 versus the 1829 book's corollary. The exact section of Fundamenta nova (reported as around sections 40-42 in secondary literature) was not confirmed from the scan. Euler's four-square identity (1748) is background only. No separate naming milestone: 'Jacobi's four-square theorem' is modern usage with no dated coinage found. person without verified work: Joseph-Louis Lagrange (developer). Fix pass 2: the 1834 Crelle paper is confirmed by Crossref; the 1829 Fundamenta nova section was not located in a record in this pass, so the 1829 dates stay unresolved.

canonicalName: Quaternions: non-commutative algebra from the geometry of 3-space
phases: Algebraic couples and the search for triplets

milestones.phase: Algebraic couples and the search for triplets
milestones.label: Hamilton treats complex numbers as ordered pairs
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, algebraic couples, read to the Royal Irish Academy 1833
milestones.description: Hamilton presents complex numbers as a two-dimensional system over the reals, then spends about ten years seeking a three-dimensional analogue.

evidence.claim: Topic page says he presented this to the Irish Academy in 1833 and then tried to define a product on 3-space.

milestones.note: Year is the date of presentation; the printed version appeared later (believed 1837, not verified in a record).

milestones.label: Discovery of the quaternion rules, 16 October 1843
milestones.work: Hamilton, private discovery and letters, October 1843
milestones.description: Hamilton realises that the product on triples fails but a four-dimensional non-commutative system works, and records i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1.

evidence.claim: Biography dates the discovery to 16 October 1843 and calls quaternions the first non-commutative algebra studied.
Article gives the same date and notes earlier four-parameter work by Euler (1748) and Rodrigues (1840) that did not treat it as an algebra.

milestones.note: Counts as precursor by the schema's public-versus-private rule; Gauss' unpublished 1819 work (published 1900) is noted in the Wikipedia article.

milestones.label: Hamilton, On quaternions, Philosophical Magazine
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, On quaternions; or on a new system of imaginaries in algebra, Phil. Mag. (3) 25 (1844) 10-13 and later parts
milestones.description: Hamilton publishes the first part of a series presenting the quaternion system in print.

evidence.claim: Crossref gives vol. 25, pp. 10-13, dated July 1844, for the first part; later parts have DOIs 10.1080/14786444408644984 and 10.1080/14786444408645047.
Article says quaternions were introduced by Hamilton in 1843 (announcement) with the series following.

milestones.note: Hamilton also communicated the discovery to the Royal Irish Academy in November 1843 (printed in its Proceedings); that earlier record was not checked, so 1844 is the earliest verified print.

milestones.label: The word quaternion in a title
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, On quaternions..., Phil. Mag. 25 (1844)
milestones.description: The new system is named quaternions in the title of the Philosophical Magazine series.

evidence.claim: Title of the first part includes the term quaternions.

milestones.note: Same paper as first_statement; counted under naming because the name appears in the title. Hamilton's own earlier use in 1843 is not documented in sources read.

milestones.label: Lectures on Quaternions
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, Lectures on Quaternions, Dublin, 1853
milestones.description: A first book-length systematic account, though Hamilton himself found it hard to learn from.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1853 Dublin book.
Biography says it was published in 1853 and soon judged a poor book to learn from.

milestones.note: Elements of Quaternions (1866, posthumous, archive.org item elementsquaterni00hamirich) is the later, longer treatise.

milestones.label: Tait's Elementary Treatise on Quaternions
milestones.work: P. G. Tait, An Elementary Treatise on Quaternions, Oxford, 1867 (later editions 1873, 1890)
milestones.description: Tait becomes the main proponent, teaching quaternion methods for geometry and physics.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue gives 1867 for the first edition scan.
Article says Tait became the chief proponent and that physics and geometry topics were written in quaternion form.
Topic page refers to Tait's work on quaternions published in 1873 and a rivalry with vector methods.

milestones.note: MacTutor cites 1873; the 1867 first edition date comes from the archive catalogue.

works.citation: On quaternions; or on a new system of imaginaries in algebra
A memoir on the theory of matrices

notes: Sources read: Wikipedia 'Quaternion' (raw), MacTutor biography of Hamilton and topic pages Abstract linear spaces and Ring theory. Tait's biography page was not fetched, so his biographyUrl points to the Hamilton page. Not resolved: exact date and venue of Hamilton's first public statement (Royal Irish Academy 13 Nov 1843 versus Phil Mag 1844); Graves' octonions (1843-45) not examined; Frobenius' classification (1878) is background only. MacTutor topic page on Quaternions (HistTopics/Quaternions) is a stub and was not used.

canonicalName: Pluecker: line geometry and algebraic curves

milestones.label: Homogeneous line coordinates in the plane
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, Analytisch-geometrische Entwickelungen, vol. 2, 1831
milestones.description: The plane analytic geometry already treats conics as envelopes of lines using line coordinates, the dual viewpoint that later carries over to space.

evidence.claim: Biography describes volume 2 as using homogeneous line coordinates and conics as envelopes.

milestones.label: Theorie der algebraischen Curven and the Pluecker equations
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, Theorie der algebraischen Curven, Bonn, 1839
milestones.description: Pluecker studies singular and infinite points of plane curves and relates the order and class of a curve in a set of equations now named after him.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1839 book.
Biography names the Pluecker equations relating order and class in this work.

milestones.label: On a new geometry of space
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, On a new geometry of space, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 155 (1865) 725-791
milestones.description: Pluecker presents the straight line as the element of space, giving line geometry in the Royal Society's journal.

evidence.claim: Title, journal and pages 725-791 confirmed, dated 1865.
Biography says his research returned to mathematics in 1865 and describes the lines-as-points idea of his final memoir.

milestones.note: Whether the 1846 System der Geometrie des Raumes (archive.org item systemdergeometr00pluoft) introduced line coordinates in space was not verified, so no earlier first_statement is claimed for line geometry.

milestones.label: Neue Geometrie des Raumes (part 1; part 2 by Klein 1869)
milestones.work: J. Pluecker, Neue Geometrie des Raumes, gegruendet auf die Betrachtung der geraden Linie als Raumelement, Leipzig, 1868
milestones.description: The posthumous book treats the line as a space element, noting the four-dimensional space of lines; Klein completed the second part from Pluecker's plan.

evidence.claim: Archive catalogue lists the 1868 book.
Biography says part 1 appeared in 1868, Klein finished part 2 in 1869, and quotes Gindikin on the four-dimensional space of lines.

works.citation: On a new geometry of space

notes: Sources read: MacTutor biography of Pluecker (Wikipedia 'Julius Pluecker' and 'Line geometry' returned errors or redirects). Open: the date line coordinates in space first appeared (1846 book is a candidate only), the date of the ruled-surface idea, and any naming or institution milestone. Derived methodological and institutional dates come only from the 1868 consolidation. Klein's biography page was not fetched.

canonicalName: Non-commutative ring theory: Wedderburn structure theory and chain conditions

milestones.label: Quaternions launch non-commutative algebra
milestones.work: Hamilton, quaternions, 1843-44
milestones.description: The four-dimensional quaternion algebra gives the first prominent non-commutative number system and the starting point for the later theory.

evidence.claim: Topic page says quaternions launched non-commutative ring theory; Cayley's matrices and Peirce's 1870 ring-axiom remark followed.
Hamilton's 1844 Phil. Mag. paper, first part, is on record.

milestones.label: Wedderburn: finite division rings are commutative
milestones.work: J. H. M. Wedderburn, A theorem on finite algebras, Trans. AMS 6 (1905) 349-352
milestones.description: Wedderburn proves that a finite division algebra is a field; MacTutor notes the first proof had a gap and that Dickson found a correct proof.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 6 and pages 349-352 confirmed, 1905.
Topic page dates the finite-division-ring result to 1905.
Biography discusses the three proofs and Dickson's role.

milestones.note: Reclassified from key_development to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1908) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Wedderburn, On hypercomplex numbers
milestones.work: J. H. M. Wedderburn, On hypercomplex numbers, Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 6 (1908) 77-118
milestones.description: Wedderburn splits a finite-dimensional algebra into a radical and a semisimple part and shows semisimple algebras are sums of matrix algebras over division rings.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume s2-6 and pages 77-118 confirmed, dated 1908.
Topic page dates the radical/semisimple idea to 1908.
Biography calls it his most famous paper and gives 1907 as its date.

milestones.note: MacTutor's biography says 1907 and the topic page 1908; the record gives volume year 1908 (volume covers 1907-08). Results are for algebras over fields, not general rings.

milestones.label: Artin extends the theory with chain conditions
milestones.work: E. Artin, Zur Theorie der hyperkomplexen Zahlen, Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 5 (1927) 251-260
milestones.description: Artin extends Wedderburn's structure theory to rings satisfying both ascending and descending chain conditions.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 5, pages 251-260, December 1927 confirmed.
Topic page dates the chain-condition extension to Artin 1927.

milestones.note: A companion paper, Zur Arithmetik hyperkomplexer Zahlen (10.1007/bf02952527), follows in the same volume; the exact content of each was not read.

milestones.label: van der Waerden's Moderne Algebra, vol. 1 (textbook of Artin-Noether algebra)
milestones.work: B. L. van der Waerden, Moderne Algebra, Bd. I, Berlin: Springer, 1930 (Grundlehren 23)
milestones.description: A textbook of the Artin-Noether style of algebra, which is the first book-length presentation found in this search that carries the chain-condition approach to rings.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record 'Moderne Algebra. Bd. I', van der Waerden, Springer 1930 (Grundlehren series)

milestones.note: Chosen as the textbook consolidation. Chapter content on Artinian rings and the Wedderburn-Artin theorem was not read; the claim rests on the title and series. Dickson's 'Algebras and their arithmetics' (1923) is an earlier monograph, but it predates Artin's 1927 chain-condition work, so it is not used here.

milestones.label: Hopkins: descending chain condition suffices
milestones.work: C. Hopkins, Rings with minimal condition for left ideals, Ann. of Math. 40 (1939) 712
milestones.description: Hopkins shows only the descending chain condition is needed.

evidence.claim: Title, Annals of Mathematics vol. 40, July 1939 confirmed.
Topic page credits Hopkins 1939 with this reduction.

milestones.label: Jacobson radical for arbitrary rings
milestones.work: N. Jacobson, The radical and semi-simplicity for arbitrary rings, Amer. J. Math. 67 (1945) 300
milestones.description: Jacobson extends Wedderburn-Artin type results to rings without chain conditions via the Jacobson radical.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 67, April 1945 confirmed.
Topic page dates the breakthrough to 1945 and links it to Perlis' 1942 ideas.

works.citation: The radical and semi-simplicity for arbitrary rings

notes: Sources read: MacTutor topic page Ring theory (saved) and biographies of Wedderburn and Artin; Wikipedia 'Wedderburn-Artin theorem' and 'Joseph Wedderburn' (leads only). No consolidation, naming or institution milestone is entered, so derived methodological and institutional dates are null. Candidate consolidations seen in the catalogue but not verified as first: Dickson, Algebras and their arithmetics (1923; Bull. AMS review 10.1090/s0002-9904-1924-03895-6), van der Waerden, Moderne Algebra (1930-31), Jacobson, The Theory of Rings (1943), Artin-Nesbitt-Thrall (1944). Earlier work on semisimple algebras over the complex field by Molien (Math. Ann. 41, 1892; 10.1007/bf01443450) and Cartan (1898; 10.5802/afst.143) exists but its relation to Wedderburn was not read in any source here, so it is a lead only. Hopkins and Jacobson biography pages not fetched; Jacobson's biographyUrl points to the Wedderburn page and Hopkins has no listed page.

milestones.label: Kummer shows unique factorisation can fail
milestones.work: E. E. Kummer, De numeris complexis qui unitatis radicibus et numeris integris realibus constant, Breslau, 1844
milestones.description: Kummer publishes an example showing that factorisation into primes need not be unique in rings of cyclotomic integers.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Kummer pointed to his 1844 example of non-uniqueness.
Archive catalogue lists De numeris complexis (1844).

milestones.label: Kummer, Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen
milestones.work: E. E. Kummer, Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen, J. reine angew. Math. 35 (1847) 319-326
milestones.description: Kummer restores unique factorisation by introducing ideal complex numbers.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 35 and pages 319-326 confirmed, 1847.
Topic page says he restored uniqueness in 1846 with ideal complex numbers.

milestones.note: Work was done and announced in 1846; the printed paper is 1847. The companion paper Über die Zerlegung der aus Wurzeln der Einheit gebildeten complexen Zahlen in ihre Primfactoren is Crelle 35 pp. 327-367 (10.1515/crll.1847.35.327).

milestones.label: The term ideal coined by Kummer
milestones.work: E. E. Kummer, Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen, J. reine angew. Math. 35 (1847)
milestones.description: Kummer names his new elements ideal (complex) numbers.

evidence.claim: Article says the term ideal was invented by Kummer.
Topic page speaks of ideal complex numbers introduced in 1846.

milestones.note: Same paper as first_statement. The exact paper in which the word first appears (1846 academy report versus 1847 print) was not checked.

milestones.label: Kummer applies ideal numbers to Fermat's Last Theorem
milestones.work: E. E. Kummer, 1847 and following papers on cyclotomic integers
milestones.description: Kummer proves Fermat's Last Theorem for most exponents below 100, then for regular primes.

evidence.claim: Topic page says he proved the theorem for all n below 100 except 37, 59, 67 and 74 in 1847.
Biography calls his work fundamental for Fermat's Last Theorem and notes the 1857 Paris grand prize.

milestones.note: Edwards' work (cited on MacTutor) says the popular story that ideals were invented to fix Lame's error is almost certainly false. The exact paper for the n<100 claim is not identified; Crelle 40 (1850) papers on class numbers (10.1515/crll.1850.40.93) are related.

milestones.label: Dedekind defines ideals and prime ideals
milestones.work: R. Dedekind, supplement to Dirichlet's Vorlesungen ueber Zahlentheorie, 2nd ed., 1871
milestones.description: Dedekind recasts Kummer's ideal numbers as subrings absorbing multiplication, with prime ideals replacing primes.

evidence.claim: Topic page credits Dedekind with defining ideals and introducing prime ideals in 1871.
Biography says ideals were introduced in supplements to later editions of Dirichlet's lectures.

milestones.note: MacTutor's biography places the supplements in the 1879 and 1894 editions; the topic page says 1871. The 1863 first edition and the 1894 edition are on archive.org (e.g. vorlesungenber00lejeuoft) but the 1871 edition was not found, so the date is unverified.

milestones.label: Noether, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen
milestones.work: E. Noether, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, Math. Ann. 83 (1921) 24-66
milestones.description: Noether unifies ideal theory of polynomial rings and number rings under abstract commutative rings.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 83, pages 24-66, 1921 confirmed.
Topic page says around 1921 she brought rings of polynomials and numbers under one abstract theory.

works.citation: Ueber die Zerlegung ... in ihre Primfactoren
Dirichlet, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 4th ed., with Dedekind's Supplement X

notes: Sources read: MacTutor topic page Ring theory (saved), biographies of Kummer and Dedekind, Wikipedia 'Ernst Kummer', 'Ideal number'. The saved Wikipedia leads file has no candidates for this event. Noether's and Kronecker's (1882) biography pages not fetched. Hilbert's Zahlbericht (1897) and Kronecker's Grundzuege (1882) are not entered. The MacTutor 'Number e' topic matched by the saved index is unrelated.

milestones.label: Lambert proves pi is irrational
milestones.work: J. H. Lambert, memoir read 1761
milestones.description: Irrationality of pi, not enough to settle squaring the circle, since some irrationals are constructible.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Lambert proved pi irrational in 1761 and explains why this was not enough.

milestones.label: Liouville's classes of numbers that cannot be algebraic
milestones.work: J. Liouville, note presented 13 May 1844, Comptes rendus 18
milestones.description: Liouville shows via continued fractions that certain explicit numbers are not roots of integer polynomials, the first proofs of transcendence of specific numbers.

evidence.claim: Scanned Comptes rendus vol. 18 (Jan-June 1844): the meeting of 13 May 1844 opens with Liouville's oral communication on classes of numbers not reducible to algebraic irrationals and starts with continued fractions.
evidence.source: Internet Archive scan of Comptes rendus 18

evidence.claim: Biography says he proved existence of a transcendental number in 1844 using continued fractions.
Article says Liouville proved his bound in 1844 and exhibited the first transcendental numbers.

milestones.label: Hermite proves e is transcendental
milestones.work: C. Hermite, Sur la fonction exponentielle, Comptes rendus 77 (1873)
milestones.description: Hermite gives the first proof of transcendence of a number not built for that purpose, using analytic approximation of the exponential function.

evidence.claim: Scanned Comptes rendus vol. 77 (1873) contains several parts titled Sur la fonction exponentielle by Hermite.
evidence.source: Internet Archive scan of Comptes rendus 77

evidence.claim: Biography says Hermite published the first proof that e is transcendental in 1873.
Article says e was the first number proved transcendental without being constructed for that aim.

milestones.note: The proof appeared in parts across 1873; exact pages not cited here.

milestones.label: Lindemann proves pi is transcendental
milestones.work: F. Lindemann, Ueber die Zahl pi, Math. Ann. 20 (1882) 213-225
milestones.description: Using Hermite's method Lindemann shows pi is transcendental, so squaring the circle with ruler and compass is impossible.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 20, pages 213-225, June 1882 confirmed.
Biography gives 1882 and says the method was similar to Hermite's.
Article says the 1882 paper was the first complete proof for pi.

milestones.note: The Squaring the circle MacTutor page says 1880; the journal paper is 1882. Weierstrass' 1885 simplification (Pi: A Source Book reprints, 10.1007/978-1-4757-2736-4_23) was not verified as a first record.

milestones.label: Hilbert's short proof of transcendence of e and pi
milestones.work: D. Hilbert, Ueber die Transcendenz der Zahlen e und pi, Math. Ann. 43 (1893) 216-219
milestones.description: A much shorter proof of both results.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 43, pages 216-219, June 1893 confirmed.

milestones.note: Role as simplification inferred from the title and length; its place in history not read in a source here.

milestones.label: Weber's survey 'Transcendental numbers'
milestones.work: H. Weber, Transcendental numbers, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (2) 3 (1897) 174-195
milestones.description: An expository survey, under the title 'Transcendental numbers', published in the American Mathematical Society Bulletin. It is the earliest title with that phrase found in zbMATH.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record 'Transcendental numbers.', Weber, Bull. AMS (2) 3 (1897) 174-195, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9904-1897-00398-6
DOI record for the same article

milestones.note: Survey role is taken from the article type and title. Its coverage of e and pi was not read in this pass. The title also serves as the first zbMATH title with the field's name; that naming use is recorded here, not as a separate milestone. Siegel's 1949 monograph 'Transcendental numbers' is a later book treatment.

works.citation: Remarques sur des classes tres-etendues de quantites...
Sur des classes tres-etendues de quantites...
Ueber die Transcendenz der Zahlen e und pi

notes: Sources read: Wikipedia 'Transcendental number', 'Liouville number', 'Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem'; MacTutor biographies of Liouville, Hermite, Lindemann and the topic page Squaring the circle. Overlaps with event H32; the 1844 milestone is classed here as first_statement and the Hermite proof as first_application because it is the first use of the analytic approach on a named target. Cantor 1874 and Weierstrass 1885 are left to H32 and notes. MacTutor says Lindemann 1880, journal says 1882. Saved leads file has no entry for this event. Hilbert's biography page was not fetched; biographyUrl is a guess at the standard MacTutor path. Retitled to match the 1844 Liouville event; the proofs for e and pi are later milestones, and P439 retains the separate pi-specific result.

canonicalName: Matrix algebra as an abstract calculus (Cayley)

milestones.label: Eisenstein multiplies linear substitutions
milestones.work: F. G. Eisenstein, Theoremes sur les formes cubiques..., J. reine angew. Math. 27 (1844) 75-79
milestones.description: Eisenstein denotes substitutions by single letters and shows how to add and multiply them, apart from non-commutativity.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Eisenstein in 1844 treated linear substitutions as forming an algebra and quotes the 1844 paper.
Crossref lists this Eisenstein paper in Crelle vol. 27, 1844.

milestones.note: The match between the quoted 1844 paper and this title in Crelle 27 is by year and author only, not by text.

milestones.label: Sylvester coins the word matrix
milestones.work: J. J. Sylvester, Additions to the articles ... On a new class of theorems, Phil. Mag. (3) 37 (1850) 363-370
milestones.description: Sylvester uses matrix for an oblong arrangement of terms from which determinants are formed.

evidence.claim: Topic page says Sylvester first used the term in 1850.
Biography quotes Feldmann that the term was introduced by Sylvester in 1850.
Crossref record for the November 1850 paper, vol. 37, pp. 363-370.

milestones.note: The title matches the follow-up to Sylvester's September 1850 paper; exact page of the word not checked. Reclassified from naming to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1855) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Cayley's first matrix paper (in French)
milestones.work: A. Cayley, Remarques sur la notation des fonctions algebriques, J. reine angew. Math. 50 (1855) 282-285
milestones.description: Cayley's first expository paper on matrices introduces the inverse and compounding (multiplication) of arrays.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 50, pages 282-285, 1855 confirmed.
Biography quotes Feldmann: the introductory paper, in French in a German periodical, appeared in 1855 and sketches inverse and multiplication.

milestones.note: Link of this paper to the Feldmann quotation is by language, venue and year; the quotation does not name the paper.

milestones.label: Cayley, A memoir on the theory of matrices
milestones.work: A. Cayley, A memoir on the theory of matrices, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 148 (1858) 17-37
milestones.description: The memoir gives the first abstract definition of a matrix, an algebra of sum, product, scalar multiple and inverse, and the Cayley-Hamilton statement for small cases; it also shows quaternions as matrices.

evidence.claim: Title, journal and pages 17-37, 1858 confirmed.
Topic page calls the memoir the first abstract definition of a matrix and describes the algebra and the 2x2 characteristic-equation result.
Topic page says Cayley noticed quaternions could be represented by matrices in 1858.

works.citation: Remarques sur la notation des fonctions algebriques
A memoir on the theory of matrices
Additions to the articles ... On a new class of theorems

notes: Sources read: MacTutor topic page Matrices and determinants (live copy, since the saved copy is truncated), biography of Cayley and Wikipedia 'Matrix (mathematics)'. Candidate not entered: Frobenius 1878 (Crelle 84, 10.1515/crll.1878.84.1), described on MacTutor as first to prove the general Cayley-Hamilton theorem; the paper-theorem link was not confirmed. MacTutor's Ring theory page dates Cayley's matrices to 1850, which conflicts with the 1855/1858 papers and with its own Matrices page; not followed. Eisenstein's and Sylvester's biography pages not fetched.

milestones.label: Liouville's first transcendental numbers
milestones.work: J. Liouville, note presented 13 May 1844, Comptes rendus 18
milestones.description: Liouville uses the way a root of an algebraic equation is approximated by continued-fraction convergents to build numbers that cannot satisfy any integer polynomial.

evidence.claim: Scanned Comptes rendus vol. 18: the 13 May 1844 meeting opens with Liouville's communication on classes of numbers beyond algebraic irrationals, starting from continued fractions.
evidence.source: Internet Archive scan of Comptes rendus 18

evidence.claim: Biography says he proved a transcendental number exists in 1844 with an infinite class built from continued fractions.
Article says Liouville proved his approximation bound in 1844 and exhibited examples.

milestones.note: Indexed in the volume table as a Remarques note; the pages (883-885 and a follow-up) were not read in full.

milestones.label: Explicit constant without continued fractions
milestones.work: J. Liouville, Sur des classes tres-etendues de quantites dont la valeur n'est ni algebrique..., J. Math. Pures Appl. 16 (1851) 133-142
milestones.description: Liouville drops continued fractions and gives explicit decimals, such as the digit-1-at-factorial-positions number.

evidence.claim: Numdam record: journal, tome 16, 1851, pages 133-142.
Biography says the 1851 results remove the dependence on continued fractions and give the constant.

milestones.label: Hermite proves e transcendental
milestones.work: C. Hermite, Sur la fonction exponentielle, Comptes rendus 77 (1873)
milestones.description: The first number not built to be transcendental is shown to be so.

evidence.claim: Scanned Comptes rendus vol. 77 (1873) with Hermite's Sur la fonction exponentielle.
Article says e was the first such number.

milestones.note: See event W94 for details.

milestones.label: Cantor: algebraic numbers are countable
milestones.work: G. Cantor, Ueber eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffs aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen, J. reine angew. Math. 77 (1874) 258-262
milestones.description: Cantor shows transcendental numbers exist in abundance by a counting argument, with a second construction method.

evidence.claim: Title, journal, volume 77, pages 258-262, 1874 confirmed.
Article says Cantor proved algebraic numbers countable in 1874 and gave a new construction.

milestones.label: Schneider's monograph 'Einfuehrung in die transzendenten Zahlen'
milestones.work: T. Schneider, Einfuehrung in die transzendenten Zahlen, Die Grundlehren der Math. Wiss. 81, Berlin-Goettingen-Heidelberg: Springer, 1957
milestones.description: A monograph that introduces transcendental numbers as a subject; it is the first book-length treatment with that title found here.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record 'Einfuehrung in die transzendenten Zahlen', Schneider, Grundlehren 81 (1957)

milestones.note: Chosen because the title names the subject of Liouville's construction. Its treatment of Liouville's continued-fraction criterion was not read. Perron's 'Irrationalzahlen' (1921) is in the catalogue but its title does not name transcendence, so it is not used.
